name: Melatonin (topical)
lead: Topical melatonin means melatonin applied to the scalp or skin as a solution, lotion or cream rather than swallowed. People who use it for their looks mostly have hair in mind: a leave-on scalp solution used as an alternative or companion to minoxidil or finasteride, aimed at keeping or thickening hair in androgenetic alopecia, and sometimes at limiting hair graying [3][9]. A second appearance use is skin: melatonin creams are discussed as an antioxidant ingredient that blunts sunlight-induced redness and photoageing [4][10][16].

Melatonin is an indoleamine hormone best known for timing the sleep-wake cycle. It was isolated from bovine pineal gland in 1958 by Aaron Lerner and colleagues at Yale, who named it for its ability to lighten the skin of frogs [1][20]. It acts on MT1 and MT2 receptors and is also an antioxidant [1]. Human skin and hair follicles carry melatonin receptors and make melatonin themselves, which is the reasoning behind putting it on the scalp [2][10].

The human literature on topical melatonin for hair consists of a handful of small, mostly uncontrolled pre-post studies, one large multicentre observational programme, and a few narrative reviews [3][4][9]. A 2023 review found 11 human studies in 2,267 patients and described positive outcomes in eight androgenetic alopecia studies [3]. A 2024 review of all topical melatonin clinical work judged the sun-protection trials to be well designed and most hair studies not to demonstrate efficacy clearly [4].

paras: Melatonin is produced mainly by the pineal gland at night, and its blood level follows a circadian rhythm [1]. It is also made locally in skin, where keratinocytes, melanocytes and hair follicle cells synthesise it and carry its receptors, so the skin is both a source of melatonin and a target of it [10]. Topical products place melatonin on that tissue directly, usually in an alcohol- or water-based solution for the scalp or in a cream base for the body.

Reviews describe two broad rationales for skin and scalp use. One is antioxidant: melatonin scavenges free radicals and raises the activity of antioxidant enzymes, which is relevant to ultraviolet damage and to oxidative stress around the follicle [1][18][19]. The other is signalling: melatonin acts through MT1 and MT2 receptors and receptor-independent routes that researchers think may influence the hair growth cycle [3][10].

Hair thinning is the main appearance use. Proponents and the clinical reviews describe a leave-on melatonin solution applied to the scalp, usually once daily, in androgenetic alopecia, as an addition to or alternative for minoxidil and finasteride [3][9]. The aim is less shedding and higher hair density over a period of months [3].
Skin ageing and sun damage are a second use. Reviews discuss topical melatonin as an antioxidant ingredient in anti-ageing routines, and as a photoprotectant applied before sun exposure [4][10].
A third, newer idea is hair color. A 2026 case series letter in Dermatology Practical and Conceptual reported repigmentation of graying hair with topical melatonin [8].

Oral melatonin is used for insomnia and circadian rhythm sleep disorders, and a prolonged-release 2 mg tablet is approved in the European Union, Israel, Australia and parts of Asia for insomnia in people aged 55 and over [1]. Topical melatonin has been tested in radiation dermatitis [6], periodontal and oral conditions [11][12][13], plaque psoriasis in combination with rosuvastatin [14], and diabetic foot ulcers [15].

In 1917 Carey McCord and Floyd Allen observed that feeding cow pineal extract to tadpoles lightened their skin, and in 1958 Aaron B. Lerner, then a dermatologist at Yale, and his team isolated the responsible molecule from bovine pineal tissue, hoping to find a treatment for skin disease [1][20]. Lerner named it melatonin from the Greek melas (dark) because it prevented darkening of the skin, and he is also known for isolating melanocyte-stimulating hormone and for work on vitiligo [1][20].

Circadian rhythms in melatonin production in humans were described in the 1970s, and a 1995 patent to Richard Wurtman of MIT covered low-dose melatonin as a sleep aid [1]. Interest in melatonin on the skin grew from the 1990s, when a randomised study in 1998 showed that melatonin applied before ultraviolet exposure reduced erythema [16]. Reviews from 2012 onward collected the small hair-loss studies [9], and the 2023 and 2024 reviews summarised hair and skin work together [3][4].

A 2012 review in the International Journal of Trichology described one pharmacodynamic study and four clinical pre-post studies of topical melatonin in androgenetic alopecia or general hair loss, assessed with questionnaires, the TrichoScan imaging method, 60-second hair counts and hair-pull tests [9]. According to the review, once-daily evening application did not significantly change serum melatonin, an observational study of 30 men and women reported lower alopecia severity at 30 and 90 days, a TrichoScan study in 35 men with androgenetic alopecia reported density rising from 123 to 173 hairs per square centimetre at six months, and a study in 60 people found hair loss fell in women but stayed constant in men [9]. A large multicentre study of more than 1,800 volunteers at about 200 centres over three months reported that the share with a clearly positive hair-pull test fell from 61.6 percent to 7.8 percent, with scalp seborrhoea also decreasing [9]. The authors concluded that a cosmetic melatonin solution could be considered an option for androgenetic alopecia and reported good tolerability [9].

The 2023 review by Babadjouni and colleagues searched PubMed, Google Scholar and Cochrane for studies of melatonin in people with hair loss and identified 11 human studies covering 2,267 patients [3]. Eight reported positive outcomes with topical melatonin in androgenetic alopecia, including improved hair growth (eight studies), density (four) and shaft thickness (two) compared with controls, and the review said the case was strongest in men; it also called for larger studies and mechanism work [3].

The 2024 International Journal of Molecular Sciences review took a more cautious reading: it found most hair studies did not clearly demonstrate efficacy, citing design limitations and the frequent combination of melatonin with other active ingredients, with one trial suggesting a possible benefit in some forms of alopecia in women [4]. Both readings describe the same body of small studies, and the reviews agree that more controlled work is needed [3][4].

Melatonin is an agonist at MT1 and MT2 receptors and a free-radical scavenger that also upregulates antioxidant enzymes [1]. For hair, the proposed mechanisms are modulation of follicle cycling, including prolonging the growth phase, and reduction of oxidative stress in the scalp, through receptor-mediated and receptor-independent actions [3][10]. Reviews of its protection against oxidative DNA damage and cell protection are available [18][19]. The single-dose pharmacodynamic data in the 2012 review indicated that scalp application in the evening did not meaningfully change circulating melatonin [9].
Hair loss: see Research on hair above. The studies reviewed are small and short, and many were uncontrolled pre-post designs [3][4][9].
Hair graying: a 2026 case series letter reported repigmentation of graying hair with topical melatonin; it is a case series without a control group [8].

Sunburn and photoprotection: a 1998 randomised, double-blind human study found melatonin applied 30 minutes before ultraviolet exposure gave dose-dependent protection against erythema, and that melatonin combined with vitamins E and C gave the greatest protection [16]. A randomised, placebo-controlled trial in 23 volunteers exposed to natural sunlight compared melatonin creams at three strengths with placebo and no treatment; only the highest strength reduced erythema significantly [5]. The 2024 review characterised all radiation-exposure studies as appropriately designed and strongly supportive of protection from dermatitis, erythema and sunburn [4].

Radiation dermatitis: a double-blind randomised trial in early breast cancer enrolled 65 patients; breast symptom scores on the last radiation day did not differ between groups, while a repeated-measures analysis across the trial found lower symptoms with melatonin [6].

Other skin and oral studies include a three-arm trial in 77 adults with mild to moderate plaque psoriasis testing rosuvastatin and melatonin [14], a trial of topical melatonin added to diabetic foot ulcer care [15], and registered trials in oral mucositis, dental implants and extraction wounds [12][13]. A systematic review of melatonin for periodontitis included four studies of a topical gel and eight of oral melatonin, all showing improvement in periodontal measures [11].

Topical melatonin is described as well tolerated in the trials reviewed, although long-term topical safety data are limited [4][9]. A randomised, double-blind crossover study in 10 healthy volunteers who applied a 12.5 percent cream to about 80 percent of the body surface found no significant effect on sleepiness, finger tapping or reaction time, with wide variation between individuals; the authors concluded it was safe for dermal use even at high strength [17].

Oral melatonin has been discussed in relation to sleepiness and hormones: a T Nation forum participant in 2010 cited several papers suggesting melatonin lowers testosterone synthesis in the testis [21]. Guidelines on oral melatonin for insomnia differ: the 2017 American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline advised against it, while the 2023 European Insomnia Guideline recommended prolonged-release melatonin for people 55 and over for up to three months [1].

Melatonin is sold as an over-the-counter dietary supplement in many countries and as a prescription product in others, with regulation differing by jurisdiction [1]. Scalp products containing it are marketed as cosmetic solutions [9]. In bodybuilding forums, mentions of melatonin are mostly about sleep and travel; one 2008 T Nation post notes the coach Charles Poliquin was said to rub topical melatonin on the thin skin of the inner thigh [22]. Discussion of melatonin as a hair-loss treatment is much less common in these communities than discussion of minoxidil or finasteride.

chain: Melatonin solution applied to the scalp
Antioxidant and follicle-cycle signalling at receptors in the follicle
Hair that is thicker or sheds less over months of use
angle.text: People apply a melatonin scalp solution once a day in the hope of reducing shedding and increasing density in thinning hair, often alongside other hair-loss products. The same molecule in a cream is also studied for reducing sunburn redness, which bears on skin appearance.
